Overview

The Dunhara Desert Region is the open desert of the [[doc-dunharargn|Dunhara Region]] — everything the walled cities of [[doc-amradadrgn|Amradad]] do not hold, which is very nearly all of it. It is the country of the [[doc-dunhartrbs|Dunhara Tribes]], and it has no fixed borders at all: what bounds it are the customary circuits of movement and the oases of right that each confederation holds by usage.

Geography

Great sand seas dominate the landscape — dune waves fifty metres high in places, walking north on the prevailing wind — broken by rocky mesas, isolated volcanic plugs and the pale bone-floors of dry lakebeds. Oases are the fixed points of the whole country: some lush and permanent, others appearing only seasonally or at the end of long wadis that flood once a decade, and all of them vital waypoints for caravans.

The climate is brutal. Summer daytime heat can kill within hours; winter nights drop far below freezing; a windstorm can bury a camp or scour the paint from a merchant's chests in minutes. The deep south sees almost no rain at all.

Peoples and Culture

The Dunhari are organised around lineage, household and seasonal migration circuit, each tribe led by a sheikh whose authority rests on hereditary legitimacy, personal standing and the consent of the tribal elders. Their honour code is exacting: hospitality is sacred and binds a tribe to protect a stranger who has eaten its salt even against its own kin, blood-feud may span generations, and the terms for concluding one are precisely codified.

The oral tradition is the region's great cultural achievement. Poets and reciters hold exalted rank, and genealogy, history, legal precedent and the terms of treaties are all carried in oral form by the tribal poets who are the keepers of law and identity. Written records, where they exist, are afterthoughts.

Politics and Power

There is no unified political order here. Perhaps a dozen major confederations and many smaller ones share the country, each with its own sheikh, warriors, poet-historians and customary circuits. They cooperate when threatened from outside and quarrel when left alone, and that balance has held for centuries.
